ssrn-7390518.abstract: Firms create value by acquiring workers who complement their productive needs, yet early applicant screening may impede this process by excluding potentially productive candidates before firms observe richer information about their qualifications and fit. We study how this friction affects firm value using staggered Ban-the-Box laws, which delay criminal-history screens until later in the hiring process. Following adoption, affected firms experience higher valuations, especially where an expanded applicant pool should be more consequential. Firms also fill vacancies faster, report fewer labor shortages, and experience fewer early worker separations. These improvements in labor acquisition are followed by higher productivity, profitability, and cash flow, while volatility, default risk, and the implied cost of equity decline. Our findings identify early applicant screening as an important labor-market friction and suggest that reducing screening-related barriers to labor acquisition can increase firm value through both cash-flow and discount-rate channels.

ssrn-7390699.abstract: By 2050, the United Nations projects that just over two-thirds of the world's population will live in cities — with almost one billion urban dwellers added along the way. At the same time, the UN changed its counting method in 2025 and thereby redrew the map of the world's cities: under the new, satellite-based delineation, the largest city in the world is no longer Tokyo but Jakarta. This paper — the third of six on the great megatrends — places urbanisation in its economic context: from the agglomeration advantages that make cities more productive than their hinterland, through the housing shortage of the rich world, to the infrastructure gap that consultancies put at more than 100 trillion US dollars through 2040. The paper covers six fields of action of the megatrend: densification and intelligent housing, the green and resilient city, smart cities and digital connectivity, new urban mobility, the demographic change of the ageing city, and the tension between growing metropolises and shrinking regions. Empirically, a twofold picture emerges: the large cities of the rich world face historic scarcity — Germany alone is short of roughly 1.4 million homes and vacancy in its metropolises is close to zero — while at the same time half of Europe's municipalities are shrinking and a third of the world's shrinking cities are in China. For investors, the paper translates the megatrend into listed companies along the entire urban value chain — exclusively large- and mid-cap names, each with its business idea and trading venues — and into an ETF selection based on a fixed checklist: physical replication, fund volume of at least 0.2 billion euros, costs, the currency question, issuer, UCITS status and exchange tradability. One central finding: an ETF that covers the megatrend of urbanisation as a whole does not yet exist in Europe — investors have to assemble it themselves from infrastructure, water, real estate and smart city funds.

en.takeaway: Use it as a starting universe when assembling a thematic basket from infrastructure, water, real estate and smart city funds.

ssrn-7390901.abstract: Market risk premium forecasts are traditionally evaluated through point forecasts of expected returns, implicitly treating the conditional expectation as a sufficient representation of future uncertainty. This paper examines whether evaluating predictive distributions alongside point forecasts provides additional information for portfolio allocation and risk management. Predictive distributions are generated using a simulation-based geometric Brownian motion framework and evaluated using both statistical and economic criteria. Consistent with the return predictability literature, the conditional expectation exhibits limited forecasting power. The predictive distributions, however, are reasonably well calibrated and satisfy several standard density forecast evaluation criteria. Portfolio analyses indicate that while expectation-based strategies generate the highest terminal wealth and strongest conventional risk-adjusted performance, distribution-based strategies substantially reduce volatility, drawdowns, and tail-risk exposure. The results suggest that forecasting models should be evaluated not only by the accuracy of their point forecasts, but also by how effectively they characterize the uncertainty surrounding future outcomes.
categories: Quantitative Methods in Investing & Financial Statement Analysis
journals: Quantitative Methods in Investing & Financial Statement Analysis

bullets: Point forecasts hide the uncertainty around expected returns

ssrn-7390998.abstract: The allocation of saving and borrowing between banks and markets and the transmission of shocks through the financial system vary widely across countries and over time. While existing work emphasizes supply-side determinants such as institutions, regulation, and intermediary technology, we study a demand-side determinant: household and firm composition and their demand for imperfectly substitutable financial claims. We build and estimate an equilibrium model of financial intermediation that uses granular household and firm data to recover how financial demand varies with individual characteristics and aggregates across households and firms. Reaggregating over alternative populations changes equilibrium financial structure and shock transmission. Differences in household and firm composition explain nearly all the 1980-2019 decline in banks' share of U.S. private-sector saving and 69 percent of the cross-country variation, but less variation in banks' share of financing. Composition also alters the impact of an increase in Treasury supply by changing which sector absorbs the new debt: under the 1980 distribution of household and firm characteristics, banks absorb twice as much, raising their cost of lending and generating greater crowding out of private credit.

ssrn-7390998.title: A Demand-Side Account of Market Macrostructure and Shock Transmission

ssrn-7391118.abstract: Many cross-sectional factors, such as industry-relative ratios, abnormal accruals, and the residual of a same-period regression, require the full cross-section of peer firms. Because firms file on staggered dates, a characteristic constructed shortly after a fiscal period closes is estimated from only those firms that have already reported. We term the resulting concern incomplete-cross-section leakage and assess whether it biases backtested performance. The conventional diagnostic, namely the disagreement between the early-filing signal and the complete-cross-section signal, does not identify the bias, because that disagreement combines three components: sampling variation from the smaller subsample, a difference in the covariate composition of the early filers, and any dependence of filing speed on the component of the signal under study. Only the third constitutes leakage. We isolate it by holding the covariate composition fixed, either through a matched control group or, equivalently, through the partial correlation between filing latency and the regression residual conditional on the regressors. This partial correlation is the selection-bias term of a Heckman model; because it is considerably less noisy than the disagreement statistic, we adopt it as the primary measure and provide it as an ex-ante screen, validated on a controlled experiment with a known planted bias. We apply the framework to two markets. For Taiwan, abnormal accruals and industry-adjusted inventory change exhibit no detectable leakage, and the associated long-short Sharpe ratio is bounded within 0.13. For the United States, where filing dates are observed directly through the SEC EDGAR system, profitability characteristics appear strongly distorted (filing latency correlates approximately-0.30 with industry-adjusted return on assets), yet the distortion is almost entirely attributable to firm size: larger firms file earlier and are more profitable, and conditioning on size reduces the partial correlation to approximately +0.09. The bias is therefore small in both markets, and the portion that remains operates through an observable characteristic that a size-aware release rule corrects. A companion paper develops that release rule; the present paper quantifies the magnitude of the bias it addresses.

bullets: Industry-relative factors need peers that have not filed yet
Early-vs-full signal disagreement conflates three separate effects
Partial correlation of filing latency with residuals isolates leakage
US ROA leakage of -0.30 drops to +0.09 once size is controlled
en.data: Taiwan financial statements plus US SEC EDGAR as-filed dates; the abstract names no evaluation window.
en.method: Treat filing-latency-versus-residual partial correlation as a Heckman selection term; validate with matched controls and a planted-bias experiment.
en.one_liner: Measures how much staggered filing dates bias cross-sectional factors, and finds the bias small.
en.relevance_why: EDGAR filing dates and financials are public and easy to pull, but this is a backtest-validation tool, not a tradable signal — hence 4.
en.takeaway: Run the partial-correlation screen before trading any industry-adjusted or residual factor, then stagger signal release by firm size.

ssrn-7391119.abstract: This paper studies how financial markets price risks associated with the AI infrastructure build-out. We construct a new dataset on U.S. data center securitizations, their underlying collateral, and secondary-market trades. We measure an AI infrastructure premium by comparing data center asset-backed securities (ABS) with otherwise comparable digital-infrastructure ABS. Since 2021, the premium has averaged approximately -16 basis points, but recently turned positive, reaching 30 basis points by mid-2026. Its cross-sectional dispersion rises sharply following the emergence of generative AI in 2022 and subsequently recedes, consistent with a period of repricing. The premium is linked to the firms driving demand for the underlying collateral: the five major U.S. public hyperscalers account for over half of annualized base rent backing data center ABS in our sample. Changes in their corporate credit spreads explain more variation in monthly premium innovations than 97 percent of comparable, rating-matched corporate-credit portfolios.

bullets: No one has priced the risk of the AI data center build-out
Spread gap vs. comparable digital-infrastructure ABS defines the premium
Averaged -16bp since 2021, flipped to +30bp by mid-2026
Five US hyperscalers back over half the collateral base rent
en.data: Hand-built dataset of U.S. data center securitizations, collateral, and secondary trades, 2021 through mid-2026.
en.method: Match data center ABS against comparable digital-infrastructure ABS, take the spread difference, then regress monthly premium innovations on corporate credit spread changes.
en.one_liner: Measures an AI infrastructure premium in data center ABS and ties it to hyperscaler credit spreads.
en.relevance_why: Good idea, but the collateral and secondary-trade data are author-constructed with no public feed, so replication is the binding constraint.
en.takeaway: Trade hyperscaler corporate spreads against data center ABS as a relative-value or hedge pair.

ssrn-7391119.title: Securitizing the AI Economy

ssrn-7391122.abstract: Many financial signals are same-period cross-sectional estimates-industry-relative ratios, abnormal accruals, any characteristic defined as the residual of a peer-group regression. Because firms file on staggered dates, a signal computed shortly after a fiscal period closes is estimated on the early-filing subsample; when filing latency correlates with the regression disturbance, the estimate embeds forward-looking selection ("incomplete-cross-section leakage"), a channel that standard temporal train/test hygiene (purging, embargoing, as-of joins) does not address. Existing remedies are all-or-nothing: release at announcement (biased for susceptible signals) or withhold every signal until a statutory deadline (a blanket timeliness penalty). We present a release-control system that grades the required cross-sectional completeness per signal from a directly estimable susceptibility primitive-the partial correlation between filing latency and the complete-cross-section disturbance given the construction regressors. Benign signals release early; susceptible signals are withheld until the cross-section is complete enough to suppress selection bias, up to the deadline. On a known-truth simulation-with the susceptibility primitive fitted on prior completed periods and frozen before gating (no oracle)-the controller releases benign signals at 36-39% completeness (vs. a 35% floor) with no detectable systematic bias, and escalates strongly susceptible signals to the deadline endpoint, inheriting its zero bias (naive-release bias -0.39). The companion analysis (Wu and Wu, 2026b) shows on observed U.S. SEC filing timestamps that the primitive separates signals whose apparent distortion is benign observable composition from those with irreducible selection; here that separation drives the gate. The controller ships as a reference implementation and is designed to sit upstream of feature-store materialization.

bullets: Staggered filings mean early-computed cross-sectional signals embed forward-looking selection
Purging, embargoing and as-of joins miss this channel; fixes so far are all-or-nothing
Partial correlation of filing latency with the complete-cross-section disturbance sets the gate
Simulation: benign signals ship at 36-39% completeness, susceptible ones wait, killing a -0.39 bias
en.data: Known-truth simulation, with the susceptibility primitive fitted on prior completed periods and frozen before gating; real SEC filing timestamps appear in a companion paper.
en.method: A release controller that estimates each signal's susceptibility, then sets a per-signal cross-sectional completeness threshold before publication.
en.one_liner: Grades how complete the cross-section must be before each signal is released.
en.relevance_why: Only SEC filing timestamps and fundamentals are needed and the code ships as a reference implementation, but it is backtest hygiene rather than a tradable signal, so 4.
en.takeaway: Bolt it upstream of your feature store to time the release of industry-relative ratios, abnormal accruals, and other peer-group residual signals.

ssrn-7391818.abstract: The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 provides for the removal of upward-only rent review (UORR) protection from variable rent reviews in most new and renewed business tenancies in England and Wales once Schedule 7A commences. This paper develops an ex-ante, state-contingent valuation framework to quantify the contractual income protection removed. A Monte Carlo expected-cash-flow model compares upward-only and two-way review rules on identical simulated rent paths, using published contemporary market evidence on growth, yields and lease structure, with volatility and rent-process sensitivities. For affected at-market tenyear leases, the geometric Brownian motion (GBM) capital-value effects are 0.47% for lower-risk logistics, 1.19% for prime offices and 3.91% for a weak-growth secondary-office scenario. Their asset-yield equivalents are 6.3, 15.7 and 65.2 basis points. Larger estimates arise in protected legacy stock and adverse contractual states: 6.85% for a legacy 25-year lease and 8.26% for an over-rented retail scenario under full enforcement. In the over-rented retail scenario, 78.46% of fully enforceable value is concentrated where protected rent exceeds 1.60 times the corresponding twoway rent. An illustrative moneyness-dependent realisability stress lowers the over-rented retail scenario estimate to 3.88% under GBM and 4.30% under trend mean reversion. Among modelled leases exposed to at least one review, initial rent state and the number of review opportunities are more informative about UORR value than property sector alone, while cash-flow duration causes capital-value and yield-equivalent rankings to diverge. The estimates are ceteris paribus expected discounted contractual values, before adjustment through rent, incentives, lease design or covenant requirements.

bullets: No ex-ante estimate exists for what Schedule 7A removes
Monte Carlo compares upward-only vs two-way rules on identical rent paths
New 10-year leases lose 0.47-3.91% of capital value; legacy 25-year loses 6.85%
Realisability stress cuts the over-rented retail case from 8.26% to 3.88%
en.data: Simulated rent paths calibrated to published market evidence on growth, yields and lease structure.
en.method: Monte Carlo expected-cash-flow model under GBM and trend mean-reverting rent processes.
en.one_liner: Prices the income protection that England and Wales will strip from upward-only rent reviews.
en.relevance_why: Score 1: a legal-reform valuation study with no tradable rule, and lease-level rent-versus-market states are not available in any standard dataset.
en.takeaway: Sizing valuation haircuts on UK commercial property and REIT exposure with over-rented assets.

ssrn-7392021.abstract: We present evidence that short sellers in the corporate bond market are primarily dealers, not speculative customers. On the day bond lending increases, dealer sales increase while customer sales decline. Concurrently, the half-spread for customer buy orders and bond prices rise, indicating that short sales reflect customers’ buying pressure. This implies that short-sale constraints that inhibit customers’ buy orders can leave bonds undervalued. Consequently, bond factors generate alphas from both long and short legs. Dealers earn positive profits by shorting bonds on average but are exposed to the risk of a short squeeze. Their short sales improve bond liquidity.
ssrn-7392021.affiliations: University of Lausanne, University of Toronto and The University of Sydney

bullets: Who actually shorts corporate bonds was unclear
Split dealer vs customer trades on lending-increase days
Lending up: dealer sales rise, customer sales fall
Short-sale constraints leave bonds cheap; both legs pay

en.method: Event study around days when bond lending rises, splitting trades by dealer versus customer and tracking half-spreads and prices.

en.relevance_why: Score 2: bond lending data and dealer-tagged trade records are both paid feeds, and the paper leaves entry and exit rules undefined.
en.takeaway: Read a jump in bond lending as customer buying pressure and screen for undervalued bonds to go long.

ssrn-7392358.abstract: Asset prices reflect not only whether an event will occur, but when. We recover this timing state from nested prediction claims on the event across deadlines. The arrival curve predicts settlement timing and separates level news from belief duration news. Unexpected acceleration raises related minus control return dispersion by 4.59 basis points, compared with 1.30 for delay. Actual deadline order adds 3.49 basis points, while predetermined business exposure locates it in exposed operations. In oil futures, resolution delay raises near relative to later delivery value. Event time is a traded state linking beliefs, firm adjustment, and physical delivery prices.

bullets: Asset prices embed when an event lands, not only whether
Nested prediction claims across deadlines yield an arrival curve
Surprise acceleration moves dispersion 4.59bp vs 1.30bp for delay
en.data: Deadline-indexed prediction claim prices, related-firm returns, and oil futures term structure; the abstract names no sample window.
en.method: Recover an arrival curve from nested prediction claims across deadlines, then split level news from belief duration news.
en.one_liner: Prices the timing of an event, not just its odds, and trades the timing news.
en.relevance_why: Scored 2: the signal is well defined, but nested deadline-indexed prediction market price histories are thin and hard to source.
en.takeaway: Build a daily timing-news signal from prediction market term structure and trade exposed-firm long-shorts plus near-versus-deferred oil spreads.

ssrn-7392358.title: The Price of When: Belief Duration and Asset Prices

ssrn-7393179.abstract: We examine whether a pooled model or a segmented model more accurately forecasts next-month corporate-bond liquidity. Using TRACE transactions from 2004 to 2024, we construct a Panel Tree that retains splits when segmented forecasts reduce validation MAE. Segmentation raises linear-model out-of-sample R^2 from 1-3% to about 24%, narrowing the gap with pooled nonlinear models, and lowers nonlinear-model MAE. The most frequently selected split variables are the mean daily transaction-price range, time to maturity, yield to maturity, and duration. MAE gains are largest for investment-grade bonds and smallest for high-yield bonds. Segmentation also lowers MAE for several alternative liquidity targets.
ssrn-7393179.affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU), City University of Hong Kong (CityU), and

en.one_liner: Splitting corporate bonds into segments sharply improves next-month liquidity forecasts.

ssrn-7393278.abstract: Water is the only economic good that nothing can replace-and at the same time one of the most underpriced. Four billion people experience severe water scarcity for at least one month a year, two-thirds of the world's river basins now carry too much or too little water, and with the data centres of artificial intelligence a new large consumer has arrived. This paper-the fourth of six on the great megatrends-examines the water megatrend from an investor's perspective: from hydrology through the economics of the value-price paradox to the investment programmes that regulators in Europe and America have already made binding.

en.takeaway: Background reading when defining a water utility and infrastructure theme universe.

ssrn-7393978.abstract: In April 2026 a humanoid robot ran the Beijing half-marathon faster than the human world record-one year after half the machines in the same race had fallen or broken down. Hardly any image captures the pace of this megatrend better. This paper-the fifth of six on the great megatrends-examines automation and robotics from an investor's perspective: from the 542,000 industrial robots newly installed in 2024, through the merging of robotics with artificial intelligence, to the question of what labour market research actually knows about displacement and new employment.

ssrn-7393978.title: Investing in Automation and Robotics: When Machines Learn to Work -How Investors can Take Part in the Fifth Megatrend

ssrn-7393980.abstract: No megatrend combines as much certainty with as much potential for disappointment as health. The demand is certain: the world spends close to ten trillion US dollars a year on health-roughly one in every ten dollars producedand the ageing of the industrialised world extends that growth for decades to come. Who profits from it is not: within the same two-year window, Eli Lilly became the first health care company in history to exceed one trillion US dollars in market value, while Novo Nordisk-in the same market, with the same class of drugslost almost two thirds of its value. This paper, the sixth on the great megatrends, examines both: the reliability of the trend and the selection risks within it.

bullets: Certain demand, uncertain beneficiaries
Narrative industry analysis, sixth in a series
Lilly hit $1T; Novo lost two thirds
en.data: Cites ~$10 trillion annual global health spending and the 2-year Lilly/Novo Nordisk divergence.
en.method: Narrative analysis of market size and two contrasting stock outcomes; no model.
en.one_liner: A strategy piece on the health megatrend: demand is certain, winners are not.
en.relevance_why: Score 1: no signal, no rules, no universe or rebalancing spec. The cited data (market caps, spending stats) is trivially available, but nothing here backtests.
en.takeaway: Argues for diversifying health-care thematic exposure instead of concentrating in one drug maker.

ssrn-7394198.abstract: Paper IV (Sun, 2026d) introduced minute-frequency VVIX as the temperature of the VIX term-structure field and derived four falsifiable predictions (P1–P4), a thermodynamic–field unification claim, and a candidate tradeable Kramers transition probability. It then reported that its own evidence — four overlapping windows, seven temperature bins each — was too underpowered to evaluate these claims. This paper further the research by using two new assets unavailable to Paper IV.

journals: Quantitative Methods in Investing & Financial Statement Analysis

ko.one_liner: VVIX를 변동성 장의 온도로 본 가설을 새 자산 두 개로 재검증한 후속 논문이다.
ko.relevance_why: 분 단위 VVIX와 VIX 기간구조 데이터는 유료 벤더를 거쳐야 하고 초록에 매매 규칙도 없어 2점이다.

ssrn-7394198.title: VVIX as the Temperature of the Volatility Field is not Enough: A Verdict on the Prelimanry Thermal Unification

ssrn-7394318.abstract: The verdict paper (Sun, 2026e) established four claims of the VVIX-temperature program survive: the sign of the thermal Kramers law, the priced NEI state variable, and a striking unexamined fact, two independent operationalizations of market temperature, a Boltzmann VIX microstructure-implied temperature Tc and a VVIX-based kinetic temperature Tk, correlate at 0.8277 (0.8288 in trading hours, 0.8286 in event time) while differing radically in observability: Tc is measurable only when the Boltzmann VIX microstructure fit gate is valid (38.4% of trading hours), whereas Tk is continuous. This paper promotes that fact to theory. We model the VIX microstructure field as coupled to two weakly coupled heat baths, the direct analogue of the two-temperature electron-phonon systems of laser physics, with coupling validated by the measured 0.8277, and we show that (i) the unification ceiling observed in Paper V (corr(G, Gfield) = 0.6718 ≤ corr(Tc, Tk) = 0.8277) is a structural consequence of two-thermometer statistics; (ii) the thermometer coverage k(t), the fraction of time the curve carries identifiable critical dynamics, is not a nuisance but an order parameter for the single-mode absorbing state identified in Paper V; (iii) the live regime (T*B = -0.0009, VVIX* = 142.94, ΔU = 5.7106) is exactly the flat-barrier state the theory predicts under thermometer divergence. We derive five falsifiable predictions (Q1-Q5), pre-register their evaluation thresholds for the next twelve months of live data, and specify the kill conditions under which the dual-temperature theory joins P1 and P4 in the refuted column.
categories: Quantitative Methods in Investing & Financial Statement Analysis
journals: Quantitative Methods in Investing & Financial Statement Analysis

bullets: No theory explained why two market-temperature proxies track at 0.8277
Borrows the electron-phonon two-temperature model from laser physics
Derives Paper V's 0.6718 unification ceiling from two-thermometer statistics
Pre-registers five falsifiable predictions (Q1-Q5) and kill conditions
en.data: Boltzmann-fit temperature Tc (valid in 38.4% of trading hours) versus continuous VVIX-based Tk, correlating 0.8277 overall, 0.8288 in trading hours, 0.8286 in event time; predictions tested on the next 12 months of live data.
en.method: Two weakly coupled heat baths drive the VIX field; thermometer coverage k(t) acts as the order parameter.
en.one_liner: Models the VIX microstructure field as coupled to two heat baths.
en.relevance_why: Scores 1: a physics-analogy theory with no entry or exit rules, and Tc requires reimplementing the author's proprietary Boltzmann fit gate, so the data is not reproducible.
en.takeaway: At most, track the continuous VVIX-based Tk as a volatility-regime diagnostic.

ko.one_liner: VIX 미시구조를 두 개의 열욕에 붙은 장으로 모형화한 이론 논문이다.
ko.relevance_why: 매매 규칙도 백테스트도 없는 물리 유비 이론이고, Tc를 재려면 저자만 아는 볼츠만 적합 게이트를 다시 만들어야 해서 데이터 재현 자체가 막힌다.

ssrn-7394318.title: Two Thermometers, One Field: A Dual-Temperature Field Theory of the VIX Microstructure

ssrn-7394718.abstract: Conditional-moment estimation and dynamic portfolio choice complement each other. Our results support this complementarity in high-dimensional multiperiod problems with transaction costs and constraints. We estimate policies from intertemporal optimality restrictions. An Adversarial Intertemporal Moment (AIM) estimator learns conditional test functions that uncover predictable violations, while a recurrent policy adapts to evolving states. The losscomparison test provides evidence against multiperiod optimality of the myopic policy at every multiperiod horizon. Over a twelve-month investment horizon, the AIM-estimated dynamic policy achieves a 25.7% annualized certaintyequivalent return in out-of-sample results of U.S. equities, compared with 12.1% for its myopic counterpart.

ssrn-7394718.title: Learning to Rebalance

ssrn-7394780.abstract: A common heuristic among index-options traders holds that sudden shifts in open interest (OI) around a price level serve as an early warning of an impending breakout. This paper tests that heuristic against a full year of NIFTY 50 index options data using a fully specified, auditable pipeline: a dynamic, threshold-based swing detector identifies intraday Break-of-Structure and Change-of-Character events at two reversal thresholds. We test three nested hypotheses. H1 (association): the PE-minus-CE open-interest differential around a break is strongly associated with break direction, a result that survives Bonferroni correction across a large battery of tests and is robust to the choice of strike band and OI-measurement window. A placebo/negative-control test addresses a specific concern with H1: that OI might simply track any sufficiently large price move, with confirmed-break status adding nothing on its own. Against magnitude-matched non-break moments, confirmed-break status is associated with a further, incremental OI reaction beyond move size alone, an effect concentrated in smaller moves and narrowing, but not disappearing, as move size grows. H2 (event-time lead-lag pattern, not a causal test): the association builds steadily in the minutes before confirmation and continues strengthening for a few minutes after, then partially declines and plateaus, the signature of a reactive rather than anticipatory relationship. H3 (tradable edge): a real-time predictive signal, conditioned to remove the confound of an already-underway price move, showed an apparently genuine in-sample edge, significant at the conventional level though materially weaker once trades are aggregated to account for within-day dependence. Every parameter of this signal was then locked and applied, without refitting, to a genuinely held-out Jan–Apr 2026 sample. The signal did not hold up out-of-sample, a pattern that is robust across five alternative definitions of the “quiet” conditioning subset used to isolate the signal from the price move it is trying to anticipate. We also went back to two specific null tests written earlier in this project, originally run on an Oct 2025–Apr 2026 dataset, and reran them against our Jan–Jul 2025 data, which those scripts had never touched. On the whole, we find no robust evidence that intraday OI repositioning provides advance predictive information about structural price breaks in this setting. The evidence instead supports interpreting OI repositioning as a state variable of an ongoing price-discovery process, informative about what is happening rather than what will happen next, and not as a forecasting signal.
categories: Quantitative Methods in Investing & Financial Statement Analysis
journals: Quantitative Methods in Investing & Financial Statement Analysis

bullets: Traders treat OI jumps near a level as an early breakout warning
Threshold swing detector flags intraday BoS and CoC events
In-sample edge vanished on a locked-parameter holdout sample
OI reacts to price discovery rather than anticipating it
en.data: One full year of NIFTY 50 index options, with a genuinely held-out Jan–Apr 2026 sample and null tests rerun on untouched Jan–Jul 2025 data.
en.method: A dynamic threshold-based swing detector labels breaks at two reversal levels; the authors test the PE-minus-CE OI differential with Bonferroni correction and magnitude-matched placebo controls.
en.one_liner: Tests whether intraday open-interest shifts predict price-structure breaks in NIFTY 50 options; they do not.
en.relevance_why: Scores 3: the pipeline is auditable and refutes a popular heuristic, but it needs intraday NIFTY option-chain snapshots and the signal failed out-of-sample.
en.takeaway: Use OI repositioning as a state variable describing the current regime, not as an entry trigger.

본표본 우위는 홀드아웃 구간에서 사라졌다

ko.data: NIFTY 50 지수옵션 1년치(2025년 1~7월 포함)로 적합하고 2026년 1~4월을 한 번도 안 본 홀드아웃으로 썼다.

ko.relevance_why: 규칙은 명확하지만 NIFTY 옵션 일중 체인 스냅샷을 확보해야 하고 신호가 표본 밖에서 무너져 매매 규칙으로 바로 쓸 수 없어 3점이다.
ko.takeaway: OI 재배치를 진입 트리거로 쓰지 말고 현재 국면을 읽는 상태 변수나 필터로만 쓰면 된다.

ssrn-7394780.title: Open Interest Repositioning around Intraday Price-structure Breaks: Evidence from NIFTY 50 Index Options

ssrn-7394858.abstract: Portfolio constraints are known to act as implicit shrinkage on an estimated covariance matrix. We show that the same constraints also compress the differences across the portfolios implied by competing covariance models, so that weight restrictions operate as a form of shrinkage across models rather than within a single estimate. As a consequence, once constraints are in place, the equally weighted 1/M combination of covariance forecasts performs on par with the best individual model, and it does so without requiring the practitioner to identify the best model in advance. We formalize this mechanism analytically by showing that the variance cost of the 1/M rule relative to the oracle-optimal combination vanishes as the cross-sectional dimension grows. Monte Carlo simulations and an empirical application to equity data with up to 1,000 stocks support these predictions. Our findings suggest that, for managers operating under the constraints they typically face, such as no-short-sales or concentration constraints, the cost of forgoing covariance model selection is small.

bullets: Model selection for covariance forecasts may be wasted effort
Constraints compress differences across competing models
Equal-weight 1/M combination ties the best single model
Variance cost vs the oracle vanishes as N grows
en.data: Monte Carlo simulations and equity data with up to 1,000 stocks; the abstract gives no sample window.
en.method: Analytical proof that weight constraints act as cross-model shrinkage, plus Monte Carlo tests.

ssrn-7394980.abstract: Momentum is among the most durable empirical anomalies in asset pricing, and since 2021 it has entered the mainstream in India. The term is applied loosely to stocks, sectors, indices, even market conditions, which obscures the fact that published momentum definitions rest on beliefs, some incompatible, about how information reaches asset prices. This paper examines ten published momentum specifications on a common Indian equity universe. The definitions span classical total-return formulations (Jegadees-Titman, Carhart), refinements (Barra, MSCI, residual momentum), and alternative measures (Echo-Novy-Marx, Frog-in-the-pan, 52-week high, Industry Momentum). We simulate them using identical portfolio construction so that diWerences in outcomes are attributable to the specific definitions. Every variant outperformed the benchmark Nifty 500 TRI, seven by margins that survive cross-sectional overlap. But dispersion within the family is significant, both on return and downside behaviour. Momentum as a family is robust in India and heterogenous as a set of implementations, but the label alone conveying little about a portfolio's likely behaviour.

bullets: "Momentum" labels ten mutually incompatible signals
Fixed portfolio construction isolates definition effects
All ten beat Nifty 500 TRI; seven survive overlap
en.data: A common Indian equity universe benchmarked against Nifty 500 TRI; the abstract does not state the sample window.
en.method: Simulates Jegadeesh-Titman, Carhart, Barra, MSCI, residual, Echo, frog-in-the-pan, 52-week high and industry momentum with one shared construction.
en.one_liner: Runs ten published momentum definitions on one Indian equity universe under identical portfolio rules.
en.relevance_why: Score 4: every definition is computable from public price data, but rebalance cadence and portfolio size are left open.
en.takeaway: Pin down which momentum definition your factor uses, and size it on downside behaviour, not just return.

ssrn-7395038.abstract: We propose and test a theory-first framework for modelling the conditional mean of currency-pair returns, applied to USD/CHF at monthly frequency over 1999-2025. Five signals-purchasing-power-parity deviation, mean-reversion of past 12-month spot changes, the real 10-year yield differential, a short-end funding-basis proxy for safe-haven stress, and the raw nominal carry-are extracted from public data. Univariate in-sample regressions, walk-forward out-of-sample validation against a random-walk benchmark, and a two-state hidden Markov model on joint FX-and-rate dynamics are estimated. Three results emerge. First, PPP deviation dominates every other single signal at the 12-month horizon, delivering out-of-sample R² of +9.9% versus a random walk. Second, an OLS combination of all five signals delivers essentially zero out-of-sample explanatory power, whereas a minimal composite of PPP, mean-reversion, and real-rate differentials generates a Sharpe ratio of +0.40 over 2005-2025 versus-0.24 for buy-and-hold USD. Third, a two-state Markov model identifies a persistent stress state occupying 27% of the sample in which USD/CHF depreciates at an annualized rate of-4.5%, and this state has been near-continuously active since 2022. The overall picture is consistent with the exchange-rate literature: theorymotivated single signals beat kitchen-sink combinations, and regime awareness is essential.

en.takeaway: Trade a three-signal composite (PPP, mean-reversion, real-rate gap) and cut USD longs when the HMM flags the stress state.

ssrn-7395059.abstract: We develop a dynamic equilibrium model of a tokenized platform with endogenous decentralized verification. The framework distinguishes miners, who incur mining costs to validate transactions, from non-mining participants, who hold tokens only for transactional benefits. Competition and subsidy-financed mining rewards generate a dual regime: with a small miner base, rents attract all entrants into mining; with a large base, rent dissipation channels entry toward non-mining participation. The model predicts a doubleS shaped adoption trajectory and a discrete upward shift in user-base volatility at the switching point. Using on-chain data, we find robust empirical support that the miner base is the primary fundamental determinant of token adoption and valuation.

ssrn-7395399.abstract: This study examines how China's Medium-Term Lending Facility (MLF) transmits to financial asset prices, focusing on asymmetric responses in bond and stock markets. Using monthly data from September 2014 to May 2025, we analyze changes in the outstanding balance of the MLF together with one-year government bond yield changes, the term spread, credit spread changes, and Shanghai Composite Index returns. A vector autoregression model is used to estimate average dynamic relationships, while a time-varying parameter VAR with stochastic volatility captures changes in transmission across market regimes. The results show that MLF shocks are transmitted most directly through the government bond market. An expansion in MLF liquidity generally lowers the one-year government bond yield and affects the term spread mainly through short-rate movements. By contrast, credit spreads respond weakly and briefly, and stock returns show only a short-lived positive reaction. Time-varying estimates confirm that the bond-market channel is more stable than the credit-spread or stock-market channels, although the strength of transmission differs during periods such as the 2015 stock market turbulence, the COVID-19 shock, and the post-pandemic policy transition. These findings suggest that the MLF affects financial asset prices primarily through the government bond yield structure, while its effects on credit spreads and stock returns are weaker, less direct, and less persistent.

ssrn-7395738.abstract: When risk must be transferred immediately, fire-sale data rarely reveal who absorbs it, at what price, or where the risk goes. On Hyperliquid, a perpetual-futures venue, a $29.76 billion bilateral census links forced sellers to recipients and post-trade outcomes, while a nested panel adds contemporaneously active nonrecipients. Receipt appears dispersed across accounts but is concentrated among incumbent market-making groups. Within the same forced sale, persistently active makers are more likely to receive, whereas temporary balance-sheet changes have weaker, less stable, and weighting-sensitive associations with receipt. Large market-making groups reduce their same-asset positions within hours. Time-zero execution costs average 18 basis points when the prior midpoint is less than five seconds old, and rise with its age. After a small positive first minute, prices move against recipients at five minutes and then recover. From thirty minutes onward, recipient-direction price paths are more favorable than those following comparable voluntary trades. Private makers normally supply immediacy; institutional backstops become important when aggregate forced flow peaks.

ssrn-7395760.abstract: Using a time-varying vector autoregressive model, we analyze daily return predictability of U.S.-dollar-hedged global green and conventional bond indices. Long-run return predictability rises slightly after the Paris Agreement for the two bond markets as a whole and, in particular, in the component of returns that moves jointly across the two markets. It rises more sharply during the COVID-19 period and declines afterward. By contrast, the relative return between green and conventional bonds shows no comparable pattern. We interpret these findings using a two-bond asset pricing model of beauty contests. The Paris Agreement provides an imprecise public signal about a small latent change in institutional participation; later public evidence gradually aligns beliefs, and persistent institutional rebalancing interacts with resale-price expectations. Positive payoff covariance gives a green-originating order a larger common-return loading than green-relative loading. The response is initially weak and gradually strengthens. Normalized calculations illustrate this mechanism. A separate extension shows that lower intermediary risk tolerance can amplify an existing response during later stress.

ssrn-7395980.abstract: Adaptive liquidity systems may have identical observable composition while differing in the redistributions that are feasible from their current states. This paper develops a constructive minimal model to examine when a mathematical representation of redistribution capability is dynamically sufficient for a specified problem. The model contains reserve, working, buffer, and strategic liquidity components and compares alternative redistribution architectures from a common initial state. Three results are established. First, a scalar aggregation of immediately admissible transfer capacity is dynamically insufficient for an urgent one-step liquidity-shock problem because it can identify systems with different immediate response capabilities. Second, a weighted directed graph is dynamically sufficient for a restricted two-step thresholdreachability problem when the initial state and transition rules are fixed across the system class, because it preserves the channel directions, nominal capacities, and path structure required to determine the relevant response. Third, the same graph representation becomes insufficient when systems with different transition operators are admitted. Two systems with identical initial states, admissible nominal actions, and weighted graphs may produce different one-step responses when the effective contribution of a transfer depends on its transition mechanism. In that context, an operator-based representation is dynamically sufficient. The construction distinguishes nominal channel capacity, immediately admissible transfer capacity, and effective dynamic contribution, and shows how information discarded by a representation may become dynamically relevant. The results demonstrate that no scalar, graph, or operator representation is universally adequate. A representation is dynamically sufficient only when it preserves the distinctions that determine the relevant future response for the specified system class, time horizon, and dynamic context. The paper therefore provides a constructive illustration of task-relative dynamic sufficiency within adaptive liquidity systems and Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT).

bullets: Same observable composition, different feasible redistributions

ssrn-7396954.abstract: This paper—the fourth and unifying installment of a four-paper arc—identifies the VIX-of-VIX index (VVIX), observed at minute frequency, as the temperature of the volatility quantum field introduced in Paper III. Whereas Papers I–III constructed, respectively, an equilibrium thermodynamic description (entropy S, enthalpy H, Gibbs free energy G), a single-particle quantum-mechanical description (wavefunction Ψ, Schrödinger dynamics, entanglement), and a quantum-field-theoretic description (deviation field \varphi \left(T,t\right), Karhunen–Loève/Fock decomposition, propagators, renormalization-group flows, Kramers tunneling), each framework carried its own independently constructed ”second-order uncertainty” variable: Paper I’s effective temperature T_eff, Paper II’s kinetic-energy scale σ (drawn from VVIX), and VVIX itself. We define an effective field temperature T_eff from the VIX-of-VIX index (VVIX), and use it to condition every construct from Paper III — the mode mass, the propagator, the renormalization-group flow, and the effective potential — on the thermal state of the market. Doing so yields four falsifiable predictions: (P1) the field’s effective mass obeys m²(T)=m₀²-γ·T_eff with γ>0, so that elevated volatility-of-volatility measurably weakens mean reversion (mode lifetimes lengthen with temperature); (P2) the barrier-crossing (tunneling) rate follows a thermal Kramers law with high R² across temperature bins, quantitatively upgrading Paper II’s ”visual evidence of tunneling” into a predictive formula; (P3) the double-well effective potential (contango/backwardation attractors) degrades toward a single well as temperature crosses a critical threshold T*, defining a phase boundary for market anarchy in which the term structure loses both attractors; (P4) higher-order (curvature-and-above) modes, otherwise irrelevant under coarse-graining, regain energy share as temperature approaches T*. The framework is operationalized as a six-layer confirmation system (adding a Temperature layer L6) and a candidate tradeable Kramers transition probability.We test these four predictions, plus a thermodynamic–field unification claim and the tradeable-probability construct, across all overlapping windows spanning May 2023 to September 2026, using seven VVIX-sorted temperature bins per window. The results are mixed, and we report them as such rather than as confirmations. P2: mean Kramers-law R² across windows is 0.816 (range 0.721–0.867); P3: mean T* ≈ -0.85 (z-units). P4 runs in the opposite direction from the prediction in three windows — higher-order modes lose, not regain, energy share as temperature rises; and the claimed thermodynamic–field unification correlates weakly, unstable and inconsistently in sign (one of four windows negative). The tradeable Kramers transition probability shows an inverted hit-rate pattern (its nominally ”high-probability” bucket transitions less often than its ”low-probability” bucket) in three of four windows. We present the empirical section as an honest audit rather than a validation.

bullets: Physics analogies for VIX term structure lack tests
VVIX-derived temperature conditions a field model
Kramers law fits at R² 0.816; P4 flips sign
Tradeable transition probability inverts hit rates

en.method: An effective temperature from VVIX conditions the mode mass, propagator, RG flow and double-well potential of a quantum-field model.

en.takeaway: At most a regime filter: bucket by VVIX and check whether contango-backwardation flips cluster in hot buckets.

ssrn-7396954.title: VVIX as the Temperature of the Volatility Field: A Preliminary Thermal Unification of Thermodynamic, Quantum, and Field-Theoretic Frameworks for VIX Microstructure Systemic Risk Management System

ssrn-7396955.abstract: The verdict paper (Sun, 2026e) established which claims of the VVIX-temperature program survive: the sign of the thermal Kramers law, the priced NEI state variable, and a striking unexamined fact — two independent operationalizations of market temperature, a Boltzmann VIX microstructure-implied temperature T_C and a VVIX-based kinetic temperature T_K, correlate at 0.8277 (0.8288 in trading hours, 0.8286 in event time) while differing radically in observability: T_C is measurable only when the Boltzmann VIX microstructure fit gate is valid (38.4% of trading hours), whereas T_K is continuous. This paper promotes that fact to theory. We model the VIX microstructure field as coupled to two weakly coupled heat baths — the direct analogue of the two-temperature electron–phonon systems of laser physics — with coupling estimated by the measured 0.8277, and we show that (i) the unification ceiling observed in Paper V (corr(G,G_field) = 0.6718 ≤ corr(T_C,T_K) = 0.8277) is a structural consequence of two-thermometer statistics; (ii) the thermometer coverage k(t) — the fraction of time the curve carries identifiable critical dynamics — is not a nuisance but an order parameter for the single-mode absorbing state identified in Paper V; (iii) the live regime ({T*_B = -0.0009, VVIX* = 142.94, ΔU = 5.7106) is exactly the flat-barrier state the theory predicts under thermometer divergence. We derive five falsifiable predictions (Q1–Q5), pre-register their evaluation thresholds for the next twelve months of live data, and specify the kill conditions under which the dual-temperature theory joins P1 and P4 in the refuted column.

bullets: Two temperature proxies correlate at 0.8277 with no theory
Borrows the electron-phonon two-temperature model from lasers
Paper V's 0.6718 unification ceiling falls out of the math
Pre-registers five predictions and explicit kill conditions
en.data: VIX and VVIX series yielding T_C and T_K; T_C is observable in only 38.4% of trading hours, with 12 months of live data pre-registered.
en.method: Dual-temperature field theory with two weakly coupled baths, coupling fixed by the measured 0.8277.
en.one_liner: Models VIX microstructure as a field coupled to two heat baths.
en.relevance_why: VIX and VVIX are public, but T_C depends on an unpublished Boltzmann fit gate and five prior papers, so replication stalls — hence 2.
en.takeaway: Treat thermometer coverage k(t) as a regime order parameter and cut short-vol exposure in the flat-barrier state (ΔU = 5.7106).

ssrn-7397158.abstract: Funding rates on perpetual futures are directional transfers, yet empirical work often enters them as absolute values. That convention can hide an economically relevant asymmetry. This paper returns to the frozen Binance BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT tape from 2020-2026 and separates lagged positive funding from the magnitude of negative funding, while leaving the increment-variance and pre-averaged apparent-H estimators unchanged. In the signed-basis specification, a one-standard-deviation increase in positive funding is associated with coefficients of-0.0058 and-0.0052 for Bitcoin and-0.0042 and-0.0041 for Ether; each remains significant after Holm adjustment. The corresponding negative-side 90% confidence intervals fall within approximately ±0.0013. Two one-sided tests also establish equivalence to zero at the disclosed, sensitivity-tested ±0.0015 benchmark. The asymmetry persists in raw units, under equal state weighting and conditional-state estimation, across alternative HAC bandwidths, and in a 499-replication 28-day moving-block bootstrap. Signed basis controls do not absorb it, and the 2020-2022 and 2023-2026 estimates show no formal break. By contrast, signed funding-by-settlement interactions and signed block-extreme coefficients fail to survive familywise-error correction. The evidence places the positive-funding result inside the increment-variance measurement family: it is a persistent observation-state association, rather than evidence about latent spot regularity, long-side inventory, causal leverage, transition information, or a trading rule.

journals: Quantitative Methods in Investing & Financial Statement Analysis

en.takeaway: Feed funding into vol features as signed components, not absolute value, and expect the effect only when longs pay.

ssrn-7397256.abstract: The low-carbon transition depends on both critical minerals and financial capital, yet it remains unclear whether green financial markets reflect developments in underlying physical material markets. This study examines the relationship between neodymium–praseodymium (NdPr) and dysprosium prices and green financial assets using weekly data from 2016 to 2026. The analysis includes a rare-earth equity fund, two clean-energy funds, Brent crude oil and the MSCI World Index, combining correlation-based networks with a time-varying parameter vector autoregressive (TVP-VAR) connectedness framework. The results reveal a persistent separation between the physical and financial dimensions of the energy transition. Rare-earth markets form a largely self-contained subsystem, whereas green financial assets are strongly interconnected and influenced by broader equity-market conditions. Shocks from critical minerals explain less than 3% of the forecast error variance of green financial assets. REMX, in particular, behaves more like a financial asset than a proxy for physical rare-earth markets, suggesting limited alignment between financial valuations and material dependencies.

NdPr and dysprosium prices vs. REMX, clean-energy funds, Brent, MSCI World

en.takeaway: Stop treating REMX as physical rare-earth exposure; model it as an equity-beta holding in the risk system.

ssrn-7397641.abstract: A growing literature reports that machine-learning (ML) models deliver large cross-sectional stock-selection gains, yet whether those gains are implementable rather than merely statistical remains contested. We revisit tree-ensemble stock selection in Taiwan, an Asia-Pacific market sharply segmented between liquid Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE) large-caps and thinly traded Taipei Exchange (TPEx/OTC) small-caps. To limit survivorship bias, we reconstruct the investable universe at each annual May formation from official exchange files, retaining firms that later delist. Over 2011–2024, tree ensembles predict top-quintile next-year returns, and we form equal- and value-weighted top-ten portfolios. Unconstrained, the random forest earns 44.6% per year against 7.9% for the Yuanta Taiwan Top-50 ETF (0050) and 6.4% for the index (TAIEX). This advantage is confined to the hard-to-trade segment. A modest NT$100 million liquidity floor turns the random-forest return negative (−1.3%); value-weighting lowers but does not remove it, so the binding constraint is the selectable universe, not the weighting scheme. Within the tradable universe the ranking skill (AUC) falls to about 0.50 and the monthly-based annualized Sharpe ratio is 0.02 against 1.29 unconstrained. Restricting selection to the main board roughly halves the return (44.6% to 23.5%), and economic capacity is only about NT$0.2–0.4 million. The collapse survives higher-capacity gradient boosting, a wide neural network, and an enriched feature set, so it reflects the investable opportunity set rather than an underpowered model: we read the evidence as liquidity-confined predictive structure rather than investable alpha.

en.takeaway: Use it as a screening protocol: impose liquidity floors and capacity caps on any ML signal before believing the backtest.

ssrn-7397641.title: Untradable Alpha? Machine-Learning Stock Selection under Investability Constraints: Evidence from Taiwan

ssrn-7397642.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being adopted for a wide range of financial analysis tasks. This paper asks whether an LLM treats references to artificial intelligence (AI) as economically informative disclosure or as a favorable narrative cue. We construct a panel of 14,336 Chinese A-share firm-years from 2021–2023. A frozen DeepSeek model evaluates anonymized Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) text along five dimensions: overall outlook, growth outlook, profitability outlook, implementation risk, and downside risk. AI disclosure is measured with a 73-term dictionary in both the complete MD&A and the text visible to the model. Within firms, more intensive AI language is associated with higher overall, growth, and profitability assessments and lower perceived downside risk. The association is strongest for growth and downside risk; profitability and implementation risk are less stable across specifications. Section-level tests locate the tilt primarily in operating discussions and forward-looking passages, rather than in risk disclosures.The scores are not merely rhetorical: favorable assessments predict higher next-year profitability, whereas growth and profitability optimism predict lower subsequent stock returns and risk scores forecast higher volatility. LLMs thus appear informative but not neutral. They extract signals about future operations while systematically rewarding AI-related narratives, raising a measurement and governance concern as machine readers become part of financial analysis.

ssrn-7397644.abstract: Using unique account-level data covering all investors who traded through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Stock Connect), this paper constructs a daily cross-border trading ratio for the first three years after the program's launch and examines the association between the cross-border stock trading and pricing efficiency in China's A-share market. The findings show that a larger share of cross-border trading is significantly associated with a lower A-H share premium, and that the association is stronger when institutional investors or northbound investors account for a larger share of Stock Connect trades. The results are qualitatively robust across several alternative specifications and robustness checks. Further analyses show that the association is stronger among A-share firms with greater information asymmetry and lower A-share liquidity relative to H-share liquidity. However, no comparable association is found for trading conducted through the QFII or RQFII programs. Altogether, the findings suggest that China’s stock market liberalization is associated with greater pricing efficiency in the underlying stock market.

ssrn-7397741.abstract: This paper examines the effect of corporate digital washing on retail investor sentiment, using data from China's A-share listed companies spanning 2010–2023. The baseline results indicate that digital washing significantly boosts retail investors' optimistic sentiment. Mechanism tests show that this effect operates primarily by attracting retail investor attention, as reflected in increased inquiries on interactive platforms, the key communication channels between retail investors and listed firms. Furthermore, media coverage of digital topics amplifies this effect, whereas analyst attention mitigates it. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the effect is more pronounced in traditional firms, non-leading firms and firms with lower information disclosure quality. Finally, we show that digital washing impairs market pricing efficiency. By examining how corporate digital information manipulation affects retail investors, this study calls for regulatory action and contributes to disclosure and behavioral finance research.

ssrn-7398058.abstract: This paper asks whether stock markets predict the economy or shape it. Markets called the 2009 and 2020 recoveries before data confirmed them, which looks like strong evidence for market efficiency. But the Dot-Com bubble and the pandemic-era gap between rising indices and struggling households show markets can price sentiment as easily as fundamentals. Through the wealth effect, corporate investment, and policy responses, market movements feed back into the outcomes they're forecasting, making prediction and causation hard to separate.

ssrn-7398632.abstract: The emergence of digital assets has challenged conventional theories of monetary evolution, raising fundamental questions regarding the long-run sustainability of blockchain-based monetary standards. This study develops a new monetarist framework to examine whether asset tokenization can facilitate the transition of Bitcoin from a constrained legacy blockchain architecture toward an advanced digital financial standard. The model integrates monetary search frictions, network externalities, congestion costs, and endogenous security deterioration to characterize the dynamic competition between a legacy cryptocurrency system and its tokenized successor. ssrn-7398824.abstract: How do residential real estate markets value large-scale climate policies? We study how Germany's coal phase-out affects residential property values near decommissioned coal-fired power plants. Combining detailed residential property listing data from 2007 to 2023 with the staggered timing of plant closures, we estimate dynamic spatial difference-in-differences (DiD) models that account for the geographic proximity. Nearby residential property values decline by 8.2%, implying aggregate homeowner wealth losses of approximately €1.9 billion. To distinguish economic from environmental adjustment, we examine changes in local employment, population, purchasing power, and local air pollution. Declines in population, employment and purchasing power coincide with falling residential property values, whereas improvements in air quality do not seem to offset these losses. Our findings show that residential real estate markets primarily capitalize the deterioration of local economic fundamentals rather than improvements in environmental quality, implying that climate policy generates substantial localized household wealth effects through residential real estate markets - a distributional channel that complements conventional evaluations focused on aggregate environmental benefits and macroeconomic adjustment.

ssrn-7399938.abstract: Does the global financial cycle still dominate capital flows to emerging markets? Leveraging granular investor-level data, this paper examines a structural shift in the drivers of global equity flows. Using a dynamic factor model to decompose flows into global (push) and country-specific (pull) components, we show that while global factors historically dominated, local factors have emerged as the primary driver of capital allocation, particularly in the post-COVID period. Local projections reveal the mechanism behind this shift as a resurgence of active return chasing: investors have become increasingly sensitive to local excess returns, re-coupling flows to domestic price discovery. We trace this shift to greater portfolio concentration among emerging markets within investors and improved macroeconomic resilience in emerging market economies. Our findings suggest that global investors increasingly differentiate across emerging markets based on local return factors rather than responding uniformly to common global factors. This deepening sensitivity to domestic conditions may expand the scope for domestic policy frameworks and, in turn, enhance the developmental benefits of financial integration by better aligning capital with local investment opportunities in emerging and developing economies.

ssrn-7403099.abstract: We propose a new methodology to estimate the equity term structure. Instead of using realized returns of dividend assets, we generalize the implied cost of capital approach and imply the term structure of ex-ante expected returns from the cross-section of observed stock prices and projected firm-level cash flows. Using US data for 1980-2024, we find an unconditionally upward sloping term structure of risk premia with rich cross-sectional patterns in the size, value and credit risk dimensions. Strikingly, value firms and speculative-grade firms have flat or even downward-sloping term structures. We also detect that the term structure flattens out in recessions.

ssrn-7403099.title: The Implied Equity Term Structure

ssrn-7404780.abstract: The public pays close attention to Federal Reserve communications about future monetary policy, but it remains an open question how those communications shape the public's expectations for the path of policy rates. We explore how market expectations adjust to the information provided in the "dot plot" of the Summary of Economic Projections, which contains the Federal Open Market Committee's assessment of the appropriate future path of the federal funds rate. The results shed light on the market interpretation of forward guidance and its efficacy as a communication tool. We find that financial markets respond to the Federal Reserve's "dot plot" projections by adjusting their expectations for future interest rates, but only partially and gradually, reflecting the understanding that these projections are conditional forecasts rather than firm commitments. Over time, both market expectations and FOMC projections for interest rates tend to converge, showing that the dot plot is informative to market participants. This gradual adjustment highlights the dot plot's role as a communication tool that shapes, but does not dictate, market expectations.

en.data: Dot plots from the FOMC Summary of Economic Projections plus market rate expectations; the abstract names no sample window.
en.method: Compares the dot plot's projected funds rate path against market-implied expectations around release dates.
en.one_liner: Measures how far market rate expectations move when the FOMC publishes its dot plot.
en.relevance_why: Dots and rate futures are free public data, but the paper gives no entry or exit rules — it reads as policy analysis.
en.takeaway: At most, fade the gap between post-FOMC market-implied rates and the dots, betting on the documented convergence.

ko.takeaway: FOMC 회의 직후 금리 선물이 점도표를 덜 반영한 상태로 남는다면 수렴 방향으로 캐리를 잡는 정도로만 쓸 만하다.
